title: Knee Arthritis Medicines: Gels, Tablets and Painkillers Explained
metaDescription: Which medicines help knee arthritis pain? Painkiller gels, paracetamol, anti-inflammatory tablets, capsaicin and what to avoid, explained simply.
intro: Medicines are usually the first step. The aim is to settle your pain enough to start exercising, because exercise is what helps the knee in the long run. Painkiller gels are often tried first, then tablets if needed. Always check with a doctor before taking tablets regularly, especially if you have stomach, heart, kidney or blood pressure problems.

sections.heading: Which painkiller gel is best for knees?
sections.body: Anti-inflammatory gels or creams rubbed on the knee are often helpful for knees and some can be bought without a prescription, says the NHS. NICE recommends offering a topical anti-inflammatory for knee arthritis first. They carry fewer whole-body side effects than tablets.

sections.heading: Do anti-inflammatory tablets help?
sections.body: They can, when gels are not enough. They are not suitable for everyone, including people with asthma, stomach ulcers, angina, or a past heart attack or stroke. A stomach-protecting tablet is usually taken alongside. Take them only as advised, for the shortest time needed.

sections.heading: What about paracetamol?
sections.body: The NHS says paracetamol can give short-term relief but is often less effective for arthritis. NICE does not routinely recommend it. Never take more than the dose on the pack.

sections.heading: Are strong painkillers like codeine or tramadol okay?
sections.body: Only for short periods under medical advice. They can cause drowsiness, nausea and constipation, and NICE advises against strong opioids for arthritis because the risks outweigh the benefits.

sections.heading: What is capsaicin cream?
sections.body: A cream made from chilli that the NHS suggests when gels have not helped. Use a pea-sized amount up to four times a day. It can take up to a month to work, and a burning feeling is common. Keep it away from eyes, mouth and broken skin.

sections.heading: What about glucosamine and supplements?
sections.body: NICE advises against glucosamine, and the NHS no longer prescribes glucosamine or chondroitin because the evidence of benefit is weak. Painkillers ease symptoms; none of them repair the knee.

faqs.q: What is the safest painkiller for knee arthritis?
faqs.a: Painkiller gels on the knee are usually the gentlest. Your doctor will choose tablets based on your health.

faqs.q: Can I take painkillers every day for knee pain?
faqs.a: Not without medical advice. Anti-inflammatory tablets can affect the stomach and heart, so they are used with care.

faqs.q: How long should I take medicines before starting exercises?
faqs.a: Only until the pain is calm enough to move. Then exercises become the main treatment.

faqs.q: Are herbal or ayurvedic medicines helpful?
faqs.a: Evidence is lacking for many. Tell your doctor what you take, because some can interact with other medicines.
